list.listitem: While adverse reactions to food are common in the population, true food allergy represents a small percentage of all adverse reactions. C
It is important to determine if an IgE-mediated food allergy is present. C

The primary tools available to diagnose food allergy include history (eg, diet records), physical examination, a serum or skin prick/puncture test (SPT) for food-specific IgE antibodies, trial elimination diets, and oral food challenges. C
The only proven treatment of food allergy is strict avoidance of the specific food. C
For patients with a history of anaphylaxis, self-injected epinephrine should be prescribed, and they should carry a MedicAlert card or jewelry that identifies the allergy. C
Oral immunotherapy for peanut allergy may decrease the severity of reaction and increase the reaction threshold at the cost of increasing the occurrence of anaphylactic reactions in some patients. A
Omalizumab appears effective in increasing the reaction threshold for peanut and other common food allergens for patients 1 year and older with multiple food allergies. B

background.definition: Food allergy is an abnormal immune response toward food proteins through either an IgE-mediated or a non-IgE-mediated mechanism, causing a variety of symptoms involving the skin, GI tract, and respiratory tract. The latter are more serious and can cause anaphylaxis.

list.listitem: Prevalence of IgE-mediated food allergies ranges from 1% to 7%.
Children up to 4 years of age: 6% to 8%.
Children older than 4 years of age: 3% to 4%.
Food allergy is the most common cause of anaphylaxis seen in emergency room visits.
Common food allergens in infants and young children are cow's milk, hen's egg, peanut, tree nuts, soybean, and wheat.
In adults, common allergens are peanut, tree nuts, fish, crustaceans, mollusks, fruits, and vegetables.
About one-third of children with atopic dermatitis have an IgE-mediated food allergy.
Food allergens are generally glycoproteins.

Only a minority of adverse reactions to food are IgE mediated or IgE associated. Characteristic IgE-mediated mechanisms occur in food-induced anaphylaxis, oral allergy syndrome, and atopic dermatitis.

Food-specific IgE antibodies bind receptors on the surfaces of mast cells and basophils that, when activated, release mediators (histamine, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes) that initiate vasodilatation, mucous secretion, smooth muscle contraction, and an influx of other inflammatory cells.
Non-IgE-mediated GI reactions are presumedly due to the elaboration of various cytokines secreted by antigen-presenting cells or T cells after recognition of particular food proteins.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: History of atopy such as asthma, atopic dermatitis, and allergic rhinitis
Family history of atopy or food allergy

list.listitem: Exclusive breast feeding during the first 3 to 4 months protects against eczema and wheezing, and may reduce the development of food allergies.C

Early dietary introduction (within the first year of life) of peanut, cow milk, wheat and then eggs at weekly interval starting at age 3 months appear to reduce risk of developing allergies to these foods in later life. A
Maternal egg consumption during the first 5 days after delivery does not appear to affect a breastfed infant's risk of developing egg allergy at age 12 months.

Early life antibiotics exposure is associated with subsequent development of allergic disorder, but intrapartum antibiotic exposure for Group B streptoccocus prophylaxis is not associated with increased risk of developing allergic disorder. Maternal dietary restriction during pregnancy and use of hydrolyzed formula milk has no role in preventing food allergies. A
Timing of gluten introduction does not reduce the risk of celiac disease. A

Probiotics administered prenatally and postnatally may reduce the risk of atopy and food allergy. A In contrast, prebiotic supplementation during pregnancy and lactation does not lower the risk of infant eczema and other allergies. A
Prophylactic medications are not recommended. C

For patients with egg allergy, influenza and yellow fever vaccines are contraindicated. A single study found that children who tolerated a test dose of 10% of the normal vaccine could safely be given the remainder of the dose. A

Skin care interventions like emollients for healthy infants during the first year of life may increase food allergy, and do not appear to prevent eczema, and may even increase rates of skin infection, based on low- to moderate-certainty evidence from a Cochrane review. B
A detailed history is essential to identify the trigger and determine whether an IgE-mediated food allergy is present, as this could pose an immediate threat to the patient if undetected. C
If the history is consistent with an IgE-mediated or IgE-associated reaction, specific IgE testing using a serum or SPT is the next step. C
The SPT should be followed by a trial elimination diet and oral food challenges to confirm the diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Lactose avoidance and breath hydrogen tests
Positive sweat test and gene screening
Clinical diagnosis of exclusion, lower abdominal symptoms, absence of allergic symptoms

list.listitem: Food allergy causes a variety of symptoms involving the skin (pruritus, urticaria, and angioedema), GI tract (abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea), and respiratory tract (rhinoconjunctivitis, bronchospasm, and anaphylaxis).

The following information should be obtained from the history: (1) identification of the suspected food, (2) the amount of time between ingestion of food and onset of symptoms, (3) symptoms attributed to the food, (4) amount of food required for the reaction, (5) reproducibility of symptoms on prior or subsequent ingestion, (6) requirement for the other cofactors (ie, exercise), and (7) length of time from last reaction. A fairly small number of allergens cause a large percentage of true food allergies: soy, wheat, egg, peanut, tree nut, fish, shellfish, and cow's milk.
Alpha-gal syndrome can cause anaphylaxis to red meat, along with gastrointestinal symptoms. This is associated with the Lone Star tick bite, which is prevalent in the southeastern US.

"Nonpriority" legumes (chickpea, pea, lentil and lupine) allergies frequently cause severe allergies, but there are significant research gaps regarding burden, allergen labeling and education strategies.Some patients with food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis only develop symptoms when food is eaten in proximity to exercise.
Typical IgE-mediated food allergy symptoms are rapid onset, usually within minutes to an hour or rarely up to a few hours. A small quantity of food may elicit severe reaction.

Practice guidelines strongly recommend use of open food challenges to aid in the diagnosis of IgE mediated food allergies. If the diagnosis remains uncertain, consider use of a blinded food challenge.
Non-IgE-mediated immunologic reactions are generally subacute or chronic.
Physical examination should focus on findings of allergic reactions if the patient is evaluated acutely, or atopic disorders if the patient presents chronically.
Consider food dependent, exercise induced anaphylaxis when there is a clear temporal and causal association between ingestion of specific foods and symptoms of anaphylaxis with exercise.

If the history suggests an IgE-mediated or IgE-associated food allergy, obtain food-specific IgE antibodies. These tests are very sensitive but not very specific. You should only order tests for foods suspected of allergy, and you should avoid a "shotgun" approach testing a large variety of foods. A test result alone is not evidence of allergy, it must be accompanied by an appropriate history.
For egg allergy, a 7 mm or greater egg white skin prick test suggests persistent allergy (LR+ 6.7, positive predictive value 92%).
A systematic review comparing skin prick tests and serum food-specific IgE testing to food challenge found that they had a similar accuracy (area under the ROC curve of 0.87 and 0.84, respectively).
The antibody titer correlates with the severity of the allergic reaction. Intradermal or subcutaneous skin tests for food are not recommended.

Trial elimination diets are useful for diagnosis and also to determine whether dietary manipulation will be successful. A double-blind, placebo-controlled oral food challenge is the single best test for the diagnosis of a food allergy. SPTs and oral food challenges should only be performed by allergy specialists familiar with food-allergic reactions and in settings equipped with the necessary medications, equipment, and staff to treat anaphylaxis.
Patients who appear to have an adverse reaction to food additives should be evaluated for sensitivity to carmine and annato.
Order other studies as clinically indicate to rule out alternate diagnoses (ie, peptic ulcer, gall bladder disease).
See for a suggested approach to the patient with suspected food allergy.
The only proven therapy is strict avoidance of the specific food. C
Reevaluation of patients with food allergy is important to determine whether the food allergy has been lost over time. C
Patient should be given injectable epinephrine and instructed how to use it. C
Patients with an IgE-mediated allergy should carry a MedicAlert card or jewelry that identifies the allergy. C
Oral immunotherapy for peanut allergy may decrease the severity of reaction and increase the reaction threshold at the cost of increasing the occurrence of anaphylactic reactions in some patients. A
Omalizumab appears effective in increasing the reaction threshold for peanut and other common food allergens for patients 1 year and older with multiple food allergies. B
Injectable epinephrine should be prescribed to patients with a history of IgE-mediated food allergy, and they should be instructed in its proper use. It is the first-line therapy for anaphylaxis.

Omalizumab, an anti IgE-mediated antibody, appears effective for patients 1 year and older with multiple food allergies in increasing the reaction threshold for peanut and other common food allergens over a 16-20 week period of treatment compared to placebo. Injection site reaction occurred more with omalizumab, but other adverse events were similar.

The only proven therapy for food allergy is avoidance of foods known or suspected to have caused a reaction. Unfortunately, a small but not insignificant proportion of baked goods contain unintended contamination with peanut protein.

Periodic reassessment of food allergy is recommended for selected patients, particularly in younger patients with allergy to milk, wheat, or egg, to determine if the food allergy has been lost over time.
Oral desensitization appears to be effective in a minority of persons,but is not as effective as food avoidance and has more adverse effects.

Epicutaneous immunotherapy (patch-based therapy), based on a RCT enrolling 362 children between 1 and 3 years old, appears to decrease the severity of peanut allergy reactions and diminishes the dose that triggers an allergic reaction. However, about a third of children, by natural history of the condition, improved without treatment. Moreover, epicutaneous immunotherapy was associated with higher rates of anaphylactic reactions. Additionally, long-term follow-up of serious allergic reactions was not investigated.
Patients with an IgE-mediated allergy should carry a MedicAlert card or jewelry that identifies the allergy.
There is significant cross-reactivity between cow's milk and other mammalian milks.

There is no need to routinely recommend that patients with chronic idiopathic urticaria or ADHD avoid foods with additives. Similarly, there is no need to have asthmatic patients avoid sulfites or other food additives unless they have a previous reaction to sulfites.

Referral to allergist is recommended: (1) for a patient with or suspected to have a diagnosis of food allergy and (2) for atopic families with or expecting a newborn to identify risk for and prevent adverse reaction to food.
Hospitalization should be considered if anaphylaxis is causing or threatening respiratory compromise.

Although sensitivity to most food allergens such as milk, wheat, and egg tends to remit in late childhood, persistence of certain food allergies such as peanut, tree nuts, and seafood most commonly continues throughout one's lifetime. C

A longitudinal study of more than 5000 Australian infants found that about 1 in 5 children who had a positive oral food challenge response to peanuts at 12 months of age no longer tested positive at age 4 years. B
The natural history of allergy to specific foods varies considerably. C
Reevaluation of patients with food allergy is important to determine whether the food allergy has been lost over time. C

list.listitem: Breast feeding rather than bottle feeding.
Early peanut, cow milk, wheat and eggs Early peanut, cow milk, wheat and eggs Early peanut, cow milk, wheat and eggs exposure may prevent Earlypeanut
Avoid smoking.
Inform restaurant workers about food allergy.

Patients with food-dependent exercise-induced anaphylaxis should avoid exercise in proximity of food consumption and should exercise with a buddy, carry self-injectable epinephrine, and wear MedicAlert jewelry that identifies allergy.
Patients with IgE-mediated food allergy should carry self-injectable epinephrine and wear MedicAlert jewelry that identifies allergy.
